# kube-agents — Build Ledger

**This file is the harness's memory across sessions and days. Every run reads it first** — before
the roadmap, before the code — to learn where the build is, and updates it before stopping. Context
does not survive a session; this file does. It is the single source of truth for build progress —
not chat history, not git log alone.

- **Source of truth for _what_ to build:** `docs/design/` (01–09). Never contradict a spec; if a
  spec is genuinely silent, pick the simplest option consistent with the invariants, implement it,
  and record it under **Decisions & deviations** below.
- **Source of truth for _how_ to build:** `docs/design/07-implementation-roadmap.md` (phases,
  acceptance, verification loop §5) + `.claude/harness/PROTOCOL.md` (the state machine) +
  `.claude/harness/invariants.md` (the pre-merge gate).
- **Source of truth for _whether it is proven_:** `docs/design/09-verification-and-validation.md` —
  every check has a stable ID (`V-<SUITE>-<nnn>`), a level (L0–L4), and a gate class. The harness
  runs checks **by ID**; it does not invent tests.
- **Project-specific values** (paths, clusters, commands, remotes, thresholds):
  `.claude/harness/binding.md`. **Durable lessons:** `.claude/harness/LESSONS.md`.
- **How the loop works:** `.claude/skills/harness-{run,verify,milestone,improve}/SKILL.md`.

**State fields in this file, and what each is for:**

| Section | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Current phase, current unit, autonomy, targets, and any active halt. Read at ORIENT before anything else |
| **Phase progress** | One row per phase: status, PR, outcome. `harness-milestone` closes a row and opens the next |
| **Verification results — by check ID** | The 09 §9.4 evidence record, one row per check run: `check_id, level, target, result, evidence_ref`. **A `pass` with no `evidence_ref` is recorded as `skipped`.** The rows live in `verification/results.csv`; this section is the pointer and the rules |
| **Deferrals** | Every check not run, with a **named external blocker**, an owner, and a promotion condition. Never a pass. A BLOCKING-ALWAYS check may never appear here |
| **Metrics snapshot** | SELF-IMPROVEMENT §6 — escape rate, rework, halts, open lessons, deferrals, coverage, cycle time. Recorded at each milestone; inputs to the improvement pass, never targets |
| **Lessons opened / closed** | Pointer into `.claude/harness/LESSONS.md`. An open lesson is a defect in the harness and appears in every orientation |
| **History** | What moved to `archive/LEDGER-phases-0-7.md` and to `verification/results.csv`, and why. Phases 0–7 progress, the suite-level Verification log, the Definition of Done, and the Outer-loop install record are all there, verbatim |
| **Decisions & deviations** | Choices the specs did not dictate, with rationale. What a reviewer reads to understand the build. Phase 8 here, Phases 0–7 in the archive |
| **Blockers** | Anything halting autonomous progress. **A halt is cleared by a human**, never by the harness |

**This file is deliberately not prettier-formatted** (`.prettierignore`). Prettier pads every table
cell out to its column's widest, which cost 64% of the file — 446 KB in 414 lines, too big for one
`Read` of the file the protocol says to read first. Write table rows with single spaces around the
pipes; nothing will re-pad them.

| Current phase | **Phase 9 — The Action Broker, dark** (07 §2), entered 2026-07-27 when the Phase 8 milestone closed. Build the **entire** safety machinery — broker, envelope, risk classifier, journal, undo plan, brake — and exercise it end to end **with no write authority anywhere**: actor ServiceAccounts created but bound to **empty** roles, every action dry-run, every `ActionRecord` a would-have-executed. That shape is the point, not caution: the hardest and most novel code in the build lands, gets reviewed and gets tested against real clusters while the worst possible bug is still a no-op, which turns Phase 10 into a permission change rather than a leap. Ten tasks, five of them load-bearing (T2 envelope + scope-derived-from-caller, T3 classifier + `ChangePolicy` that may only tighten, T4 undo-plan generation whose "cannot generate" path **reclassifies the action as gated**, T6 the brake, which must work through `kubectl` with inference down, T9 the consolidated gate). **PLAN landed 2026-07-27: [`docs/build/phase-9.md`](phase-9.md)** — survey (the pipeline is greenfield: five CRDs, a second binary, a second image, a second Deployment per CR, none of which exist), the Accept→check binding, the ten-unit breakdown, deferrals, and IMPLEMENT notes. It resolves **four planning defects** before any code: **(1)** 07 §2's "bound to **empty** roles" is literally incompatible with journalling — 06 §2.2.1's broker operations grant is what lets the broker authenticate (step 1), read the brake (step 5) and write the journal (step 11), and omitting it "does not fail safe — it bricks the tier"; so "empty" means empty of _tenant_ authority and Accept (e)'s sweep becomes the two-sided **V-BRK-013** assertion. **(2)** V-BRK/V-REV/V-ISO are **BLOCKING-ALWAYS and may not be deferred** (09 §9.6), yet ~11 of their checks need a real mutation that dark mode forbids — resolved by one code path and two RBAC profiles, with a test-only tenant overlay confined to `dev/` by a new `invariants-gate.py` check, rather than by shipping checks that cannot fail (V-MET-014). **(3)** V-BRK-003 needs an audit-log stream GKE only exposes through Cloud Logging, with Data Access logs off by default — the reconciler takes a pluggable audit source and P9-T1 opens with the probe. **(4)** Accept (a)–(e) does not cover the ratchet: V-RUN (14) and V-ISO-001/002/006 are 17 required checks no Accept bullet names, so the gate runs the ratchet and Accept is the subset 07 chose to print. _Prior phase:_ **Phase 8 — Contain the pod, close the boundary, make the install real**, ✅ merged via [#30](https://github.com/adamparco/kube-agents/pull/30); it added no imperative capability, it removed the reasons starting would be unsafe. Breakdown and evidence: `docs/build/phase-8.md`, the Phase progress row below, and [`archive/LEDGER-phases-0-7.md`](archive/LEDGER-phases-0-7.md) §Status for everything before it. |
| Current task | **P9-T7d-1 is done — the mesh trust root, and the discovery that the agent's certificate is half of the broker's identity check rather than just its transport.** 08 §2.3 asks for mutual TLS between the two halves of the pair; T7b rendered Deployments that mount `<agent>-broker-tls` and `<agent>-mesh-tls` and left them fail-closed at `BrokerReady: false` because nothing filled them. This unit fills them. `config/mesh-ca/` adds the three-object chain a CA needs — a `selfSigned` `ClusterIssuer`, a `isCA` `Certificate` in **cert-manager's** namespace, and the `kubeagents-mesh-ca` `ClusterIssuer` that signs every leaf in the fleet — and `internal/controller/mesh_trust.go` renders the two leaves per Agent. **A `ClusterIssuer`, not an `Issuer` per namespace, and the reason is the private key.** Agents live in many namespaces and the mesh spans all of them, so every pair must chain to the same root; a namespaced `Issuer` needs the CA Secret present in every namespace hosting an agent, which puts the **CA private key** in every tenant namespace, readable by whatever that tenant's RBAC grants — one compromised namespace then mints a valid mesh identity for any workload in the fleet. Here the key stays where cert-manager runs and only leaves leave. **One CA signing everyone is not one authorization for everyone**, and that is checked rather than assumed: the broker still authenticates by TokenReview against a projected token with audience `kubeagents-broker`, still compares the result to the single `ExpectedCaller` it serves, and still refuses on `PeerMismatch`. Membership of the mesh and permission to act are two claims proved by two credentials. **The unit's most consequential finding is a string.** `auth.go` refuses unless the client certificate's SPIFFE URI SAN equals the identity it derived independently from the token, so the renderer and the verifier must agree **exactly** — and two `Sprintf`s with the same format string are two definition sites that agree until one is edited. `broker.SPIFFEID` is now exported and called by both; the test pins that they agree **and** that the agreed shape is canonical, because two callers of the same wrong function agree perfectly. Had this been off by a separator, every envelope in the fleet would have been refused at the transport layer with a message about trust domains, visible only at L2 after a rollout, looking exactly like a certificate fault. **The two ends are asymmetric on purpose and the tests say so**: the broker leaf carries `server auth` and a dnsName equal to the SAN the agent pins, and **not** `client auth`; the agent leaf carries `client auth` and no dnsNames at all, because it is never dialled. Both are ECDSA-256 with `rotationPolicy: Always` — a certificate that reuses its key on renewal has not renewed the thing that matters. **The controller creates `Certificate`s and never touches a `Secret`**, which is what keeps 08 §2.7's "no read verb on Secrets" intact while still delivering key material to the pod: cert-manager owns the write, the kubelet does the mount, and the operator's new RBAC is one rule on `cert-manager.io/certificates`. **cert-manager's Go types are deliberately not a dependency** — `go get` on them upgraded every `k8s.io/*` module and added `gateway-api` in exchange for four struct literals, so the leaves are `unstructured` applied server-side, and cert-manager's *absence* is a `RESTMapper` probe and a logged skip rather than an error: no mesh CA installed means no Secrets, means `BrokerReady: false`, means an agent that runs read-only and says why (08 §2.4), which is the fail-closed direction — whereas erroring would wedge the reconciler for every Agent in a cluster that simply chose not to install the mesh. **Two uniqueness domains, not one, found by rendering two CRs and not one** ([[LSN-015]] again): `Certificate` names and `secretName`s key on `agent.Name` and are unique for free, but the actor SPIFFE ID keys on `(tier, scope)` and is unique **only because admission refuses a duplicate pair** — my first fixture gave two Agents the same tier and scope and the collision test correctly reported one mesh identity claimed by two CRs. The renderer cannot see that; the webhook is what holds the line, and the test now says so in place. **A check from an earlier unit fired again and was again right.** `pause-is-not-scale-to-zero.py` property 5 refused to classify the new file; `mesh_trust.go` is filed under `RENDERING` — the **strict** arm — rather than `EXEMPT`, because the wrong implementation it forecloses is a bad one: withholding a certificate from a paused agent takes the pair's **transport** down, which reads fleet-wide as a broker outage and drops the agent into observe-and-report (08 §2.4) instead of letting it refuse with a reason (06 §4.4). **Claims no new check ID** — T7d-1's properties are the L1 property tests in `mesh_trust_test.go` (six, all green); 09's mesh assertions are V-ISO's and are L2, routed to P9-T9. Gates: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` all green, **L0 26/26**, `invariants-gate.py` 15/15, prettier clean over the branch changed set. **Next: P9-T7d-2** — the broker ingress NetworkPolicy, the agent's egress-to-broker rule, the actor ServiceAccounts bound to 06 §2.2.1's empty role, and the derived `examples/gitops-repo/` exemplars: GitOps artifacts and the provisioning path, no reconciler code, because P1-T4/T5 already ruled that the controller does not mint identities and the actor SA is the higher-authority half. |

**Load-bearing halt conditions (stop and surface, do NOT merge or auto-advance):**

1. A **security negative test** (03 §11) fails — read-only, per-tier scope, attenuation, no break-glass.
2. A **failure-isolation chaos test** (05 §8) fails.
3. An **invariant** (`.claude/harness/invariants.md`) would be violated by the change.
4. A destructive test is about to run against a context that is not an anchored **`gke-scratch-*`**.
5. A spec conflict with no simplest-option resolution.

The 31-case 09 §7.3 round-trip corpus was written from the spec's table, not from `strategy.go`, and the cross-package invariant found **thirteen irreversible cloud deletes classifying `routine`** ([[LSN-033]]). **V-REV-003 and V-REV-004 claimed at L1**; their L2 instances, and V-REV-001/V-REV-009, wait on an executor that does not exist yet. **T5a done 2026-07-27** ([#37](https://github.com/adamparco/kube-agents/pull/37)) — the write path: `internal/broker/execute/` with the field manager and its inverse, the one diff used at both ends of the pipeline, the classify/execute integrity check, all-or-nothing snapshot capture, the executor's three orderings, and the API-server-backed `Reader`/`Applier`, proven by 6 envtest cases against a real API server. **T5 was split because the row is two deliverables** — the write, and everything that happens after it — the same seam as T3a/T3b and P8-T8a/b/c. **The headline is that the diff's own granularity was a gate bypass.** A map key absent on one side produced one whole-value op — `add /metadata/annotations` carrying the whole block — which is *correct* for the integrity check, because the same function computes both sides and both are coarse in the same places. But the diff has a second consumer: it is what `when.fieldPaths` is matched against, and `PointerPrefixMatch` requires the **rule** to be the prefix. A rule naming `metadata.annotations['kube-agents/restarted-at']` is *longer* than `/metadata/annotations`, so it does not fire — "set the whole annotations block in one apply" becomes a way to write a gated annotation without tripping the gate, silently. Recorded as **[[lsn-034]]**: a value compared against itself will never tell you it is the wrong shape, so the precision bar belongs to whichever consumer compares it to a string a human wrote. Mechanized by `assertLeafOps`, mutation-tested on both the add and remove arms, with a paired negative that stays green under the mutation. **Claimed: V-BRK-020 at L1 and nothing else.** V-BRK-006 is `L2, L4`; V-BRK-018 and V-BRK-019 are `L2`; V-REV-002 is `L2` and phase 10 — the properties are implemented and asserted here, but **a property proven at a level the check does not list is not that check passing**, and all four go to `broker-execute-l2.sh` in P9-T9. **Next: T5b** — the per-kind verification predicates of 04 §5.1, the recovery ladder, automatic rollback and the selector fan-out. Opened by the Phase 8 milestone. **The whole safety machinery, exercised end to end with no write authority anywhere** — actor SAs bound to empty roles, broker in dry-run, journal recording would-have-executed. It is the ordering constraint in 07 §5 made concrete: broker, classifier, journal and undo must exist and be tested **before** any agent gets a write verb (Phase 10), so the novel code lands while the worst bug it can produce is a no-op. Acceptance in 07 §2; **T10 done 2026-07-27** — the carried credential seam, closed with **V-CMP-006** as `dev/test_mcp_env_declared.py` (L0, negative control included); L3 confirmation still pending a live rebuild. **Task breakdown written 2026-07-27 to [`docs/build/phase-9.md`](phase-9.md)** — ten units, five load-bearing, and four planning defects resolved before any code (the "empty roles" / journalling contradiction; ~11 BLOCKING-ALWAYS checks that need a mutation dark mode forbids; V-BRK-003's audit-log source; and 17 ratchet checks no Accept bullet names). **Two items carried in from Phase 8, both user-reported against the live install:** **P9-T10** — the `agent_common` MCP server is declared with no `env:` block in either definition site, so `API_SERVER_KEY` never reaches the process implementing `call_agent`, and `/cluster-admin` never answers; new check **V-CMP-006**. (Its sibling, `call_agent` hardcoded to `^(platform)$` so hub→spoke dispatch has no code path in any tier, stays an amended **P15-T1**.) Rationale and the two traps that make this look fixed when it is not: **Decisions & deviations**, top row. |

## Verification results — by check ID (09 §9.4)

One row per **check** run, keyed by its stable ID from `docs/design/09-verification-and-validation.md`
§6. Written by `harness-verify`. **The table moved to [`../../verification/results.csv`](../../verification/results.csv)
on 2026-07-26** — 37 rows moved byte-identically, 41 now, the 09 §9.4 shape it always had
(`date, phase, check_id, level, target, result, evidence_ref, notes`). It was 105 KB of the ledger and
nothing reads it during ORIENT; a CSV is the format 09 §9.4 asks for anyway.

`evidence_ref` points at the real artifact — command output, the denial message, an `ActionRecord`
ID, an audit-log query. **A `pass` with no `evidence_ref` is recorded as `skipped`, not as a pass.**
Keep the most recent result per `(check_id, level, target)`. A full run additionally emits the
machine-readable manifest at `verification/manifest-<phase>-<YYYYMMDD>.csv` with the complete 09 §9.4
field set (`requirement_ids[]`, `duration_s`, `started_at`, `image_digests[]`, `notes`).

**Two drifts are carried across rather than laundered, because normalizing them would be inventing
results.** The `result` column holds `correction` and `finding` on ten rows; 09 §9.4's enum is
`pass | fail | deferred | skipped | quarantined` and neither word is in it. Five `(check_id, level,
target)` keys appear twice, against the keep-the-most-recent rule directly above, and every row
carries the same date, so which one is most recent is not recoverable. Both are for the next full run
to write correctly, not for this move to guess at. The `target` column records `kind*` throughout:
that is what those runs actually ran on, and history does not get retconned by a substrate change.

## Deferrals

Every check that could not run, with a **named external blocker**. Deferred is a first-class result:
it is never reported as passing, and reclassifying a failure as a deferral is a named reward hack
(SELF-IMPROVEMENT §4). **A BLOCKING-ALWAYS check may not be deferred** — if it cannot run, the build
is not verifiable, and that is a halt (09 §9.6). Reviewed at every improvement pass; promote any row
whose blocker has cleared.

The store is `.claude/harness/LESSONS.md`; this is the pointer and the running count. An **open
lesson is a defect in the harness**. Over the `binding.md` threshold (**5**), the next invocation is
an improvement pass and nothing else. A lesson open across three passes escalates to a human.

Only this table did not hear about it | **closed** (mechanized) | Found by an audit of the harness's own metrics, not by the harness: the row above still said `**open**` while the summary 34 lines up said `0 of 28`, and no check compares the two. A count that is asserted in three files is a count with three chances to be wrong — `LESSONS.md`'s index is the ONE definition site, and both LEDGER summaries and this table are derived views that must name it. Recorded rather than silently fixed, because the failure here is not the stale word, it is that the contradiction survived every read of a file the protocol opens first |

The diff has a second consumer: `when.fieldPaths` matching, where `PointerPrefixMatch` requires the **rule** to be the prefix. A rule naming one annotation inside a newly-created block is *longer* than the coarse op's path and cannot fire, so "ensure there is no annotations block, then set the whole block in one apply" writes a gated annotation without tripping the gate — silently. Found by two tests aimed elsewhere (`~1` escaping; loud truncation, which reported `Truncated=false` for 250 added labels because they were one op); neither was about granularity and neither said so. **Generalization:** a self-relative consumer cannot detect a systematic error, because a systematic error cancels — so the precision bar for a derived value belongs to whichever consumer compares it to something outside the process, even when that is not the reason the value exists. [[lsn-032]]'s geometry one level in. Mechanized by **`assertLeafOps`** + `TestDiffEmitsOnlyLeafOps` in `k8s-operator/internal/broker/execute/diff_test.go`, run on every PR by `k8s-operator-test.yml`: checkable on a single op with no reference to any other diff, asserted on both the add and remove arms, and mutation-tested by stubbing `subtreeOps` to return nothing. | 2026-07-27 | **LSN-035** | P9-T5b — a mutation survived, and the rule it broke turned out to be one no input can reach | **open** | Mutation-testing the ¬ negative controls for V-PRO-021 killed 9 of 11 invariants; the 2 survivors were **the two properties the check text names by hand**. Not missing tests — both rules had tests and both passed for an unrelated reason, because every history written to enter rung 2 twice had to *descend* to do it and the non-decreasing rule rejected it first. **A test that asserts "this is rejected" cannot tell you which rule did the rejecting.** Deeper: within a chain-valid history the two rules are **logically unreachable** — monotonicity plus no-self-transition already imply both — so no better history exists to write. The general finding is that a **redundant** guard and an **unenforced** guard are indistinguishable from a green suite, and mutation testing reports them identically as a survivor; a survivor is therefore a question (*is this rule reachable?*) whose two answers need opposite responses, and "add a test for the surviving rule" answers neither. Where `¬` requires a negative control, that control only ever proves the **suite** fails, never **which rule** made it fail — so where rules overlap, the narrow ones silently stop carrying their weight. **Not closed here.** The ladder was repaired by moving assertions off the rules and onto the properties (`TestLadderPropertiesHoldOverEveryAcceptedHistory`, all 1554 histories of length ≤ 4, accepted count pinned at exactly 30, re-mutated to confirm it is what now kills monotonicity), and both derived rules were **kept** with the finding written into `ladder.go` — the implication runs one way, and a rule deleted for redundancy is one nobody restores when the premise changes. But exhaustive enumeration only worked because the state space is tiny, so it is not the general mechanization. Candidates for the next `harness-improve`: require every ¬ check to record *which* rule its negative control exercised and assert the error names it, or make reachability an explicit written question a survivor must answer before it may be allowlisted. Sibling of [[lsn-032]] and [[lsn-033]] — **a check that shares a premise with the thing it checks cannot see a defect in the premise**. |

T7d has to introduce a mesh CA `ClusterIssuer` and a CA `Certificate` under it first, which is a cert-manager API-types dependency and a cluster-scoped object, not a line in `broker_manifests.go`. | 2026-07-28 | 9 | **The SPIFFE ID string has exactly one definition site: `broker.SPIFFEID(trustDomain, ns, sa)`, exported from `internal/broker/auth.go` and called by the renderer as well as the verifier.** The renderer does not `Sprintf` its own copy. | The mesh certificate is not just the pair's transport — **it is half of the broker's identity check.** `auth.go` refuses an envelope with `ReasonPeerMismatch` unless the client certificate's SPIFFE URI SAN equals the identity it derived independently from the TokenReview on the projected token. Two `fmt.Sprintf`s with the same format string are not one definition site; they are two, and they agree until one is edited. Had the renderer emitted any other shape — a different separator, a trailing slash, the tier instead of the ServiceAccount — **every envelope in the fleet would be refused at the transport layer**, with a message about trust domains, discoverable only at L2 after a full rollout, and looking exactly like a certificate problem rather than a string problem. The test pins both halves of the claim: that the two sides agree, *and* that the agreed shape is the canonical `spiffe://<td>/ns/<ns>/sa/<sa>` — because two callers of the same wrong function agree perfectly. | 08 §2.3; 06 §2.2.1 |

| 2026-07-28 | 9 | **The broker env vars are merged LAST, and the broker image is not a CR field.** | Both are the same question — who chooses what sits behind the actor credential — and the first was a live bug in this unit's first draft. | 2026-07-28 | 9 | **The broker's kubelet probes are `tcpSocket`, and the real mTLS health check runs in the agent's init container.** | Not a weakening — a consequence of `tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert`. The kubelet's `httpGet` prober holds no client certificate, so every probe would fail the handshake and it could not distinguish a down broker from an unauthenticated caller; using `httpGet` would mean either turning client-cert verification off or accepting a permanently-failing readiness probe. `tcpSocket` on 8443 proves the port is bound and is documented at the site as proving nothing about TLS. The check that matters runs where the certificate is: the agent pod's `wait-for-broker` init container, which does a real mTLS GET of `/healthz` with the SAN pinned explicitly rather than inferred from the URL host. It runs the **broker image** — already built, protocol-matched, no shell — because the agent's Python harness image has no guaranteed TLS-capable client on PATH. | 08 §2.4, §2.6 |
| 2026-07-28 | 9 | **`wait-for-broker` always exits 0; a configuration fault writes no verdict at all.** | 08 §2.4: on timeout the agent starts anyway in observe-and-report mode, because a broker outage must not blind the fleet. A non-zero exit is `Init:CrashLoopBackOff`, which takes the agent's READ path down with its write path — the one outcome the section rules out — so the verdict is a file the agent reads, not an exit code the kubelet acts on. This is not a fail-open: the agent holds no write verb of its own (03 §11), so "started without a broker" means "cannot write" because RBAC says so, not because the process chose to behave. Two corollaries are deliberate. Exiting 0 with **no** verdict would be the real fail-open (the agent finds no file and has to guess, and the safe guess is not the obvious one), so cancellation mid-wait still records `unavailable`. And a **configuration** fault — a missing flag, an unreadable certificate — is the one loud case, returning an error and writing nothing, because `unavailable` there would read as a broker outage and send whoever debugs it at the wrong half of the pair. | 08 §2.4 |

| 2026-07-28 | 9 | **`RenderScope` digests a length-prefixed canonical encoding, not the readable join — and pass-through requires DNS-1123 levels** | Found by the unit's own corpus, not reasoned out in advance. The first draft hashed `ScopeKey`, the readable `<project>.<cluster>.<namespace>` join, which is ambiguous: `{acme, prod.eu, payments}` and `{acme, prod, eu.payments}` produce one string. Both were also short and legal, so both took the pass-through path and the digest never ran — the collision was in rule 1, not rule 2. The fix is two-sided: hash `canonical(s)` (`len:value` per level, injective for any level content including one containing the separator), and require `IsWellFormed()` plus every non-empty level to be a DNS-1123 label before allowing pass-through. The well-formedness clause is not decoration — without it the malformed `{cluster: c}` and the ordinary `{project: c}` both join to `"c"`. Rule 3 (`looksHashed`) keeps the two output sets disjoint, so injectivity is an argument with a stated residual (a 40-bit digest collision between two scopes also sharing a 52-byte prefix) rather than a property that happened to hold on the cases someone thought of. | 08 §2.5 | — |

| 2026-07-27 | 9 | **Row 8's contested exemption for undo, and why the index excludes UID** | Undo is exempt from the contested rule because the marker is created **by** undo: refusing an undo against a contested target would make `contested` an unrecoverable state, reachable only by the control it disables. The field lives on `Refusal` rather than being computed at the write site because only the brake knows whether a refusal is temporary — a value derived at the HTTP boundary would be derived from the status code, which cannot distinguish a freeze that clears in an hour from one with no expiry at all. Pause answers **60 s**: short enough that the first retry after a human types `resume` lands promptly, long enough that a paused agent with a full queue does not turn a pause into a request flood against the thing an operator is trying to calm down. A freeze answers with the seconds until its own `expiresAt`, **capped at one hour** — a three-day freeze telling a caller to sleep for three days converts a cleared freeze into an agent that is still, as far as anyone can see, frozen.
